prompt: What does `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` start that the default `MOCK` does not?
hint: Think about what a request has to cross to reach the controller.

choices.text: A second PostgreSQL container, on a port of its own
choices.why: The database comes from `TestcontainersConfiguration` in both cases. The port in `RANDOM_PORT` is the web server's.

choices.text: The embedded Tomcat, listening on a free port the OS picks
choices.why: Right. `MOCK` has no server at all; `RANDOM_PORT` starts Tomcat on whatever port is free, and `@LocalServerPort` says which.

choices.text: A `MockMvc` that calls the controller in the same thread
choices.why: That is how requests reach the controller under `MOCK`, with no socket.

choices.text: A separate JVM running `target/bookshop-0.1.0.jar`
choices.why: Everything runs inside the JVM failsafe started; no jar is launched.

prompt: Why does `BooksApiIT` ask for `RANDOM_PORT` rather than `DEFINED_PORT`?

choices.text: `DEFINED_PORT` starts the application without its security filter chain
choices.why: Both start the same application with the same filters. They differ only in the port.

choices.text: A random port makes the context start faster
choices.why: Choosing a port costs nothing measurable; the context and the container are the slow parts.

choices.text: Another program on 8080 would fail the test, not the code
choices.why: Right. `DEFINED_PORT` uses `server.port`, and a test that fails because another process holds it fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the code.

choices.text: Testcontainers refuses to start next to a server on a fixed port
choices.why: Testcontainers maps the database's port and never looks at the web server's.

prompt: A colleague tests the API by building a `BookController` and calling `get(1)` directly. Which of these does that test never exercise, where `BooksApiIT` does? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The mapping from `GET /books/1` to the method
choices.why: Right. The direct call skips the dispatcher that finds the method from the path.

choices.text: The security filter chain
choices.why: Right. Filters run around a request, and a method call is not one.

choices.text: Jackson writing the answer as JSON
choices.why: Right. The method returns a record; only the HTTP layer turns it into JSON.

choices.text: `BookService` looking the book up
choices.why: The controller calls the service in both tests, so both run it.

choices.text: The `get` method's own code
choices.why: That is the one thing the direct call does run.

prompt: REST Assured 6.1.0's pom asks for Groovy 5.0.3, and `mvn dependency:tree` shows Groovy 5.0.8. Why?

choices.text: Maven always resolves a library to the newest version available
choices.why: Maven never looks for newer versions on its own. Left alone, it would have taken 5.0.3.

choices.text: Spring Boot's parent manages Groovy, and the managed version wins
choices.why: Right. The parent's `<dependencyManagement>` from lesson 4 names a version for Groovy, and it applies even to a library that arrives through somebody else's pom.

choices.text: The `rest-assured.version` property raised Groovy along with REST Assured
choices.why: That property is only used by the REST Assured dependency; it says nothing about Groovy.

choices.text: Hamcrest 3.0 from the test starter requires Groovy 5.0.8
choices.why: Hamcrest has no dependency on Groovy at all.

prompt: Put in order what happens after `mvn verify -Dit.test=BooksApiIT`, up to the first request.
hint: The unit tests come from an earlier phase of the lifecycle.
items: Tomcat starts on a random port

prompt: In the detour, the failure ended with `at com.example.bookshop.BooksApiIT.anUnknownBookIsAProblemDetail(BooksApiIT.java:50)`. What is on line 50?

choices.text: The `get("/books/{id}", 999)` that sent the request
choices.why: The request was sent and answered without trouble; it was a claim about the answer that broke.

choices.text: The line of `ApiErrorHandler` that wrote the problem detail
choices.why: That code runs in the server. The stack trace is the test's own thread, checking the answer.

choices.text: The `contentType(...)` expectation that did not match
choices.why: Right. REST Assured fails at the expectation, so the line number points at the claim that broke.

choices.text: The first line of the test method
choices.why: A stack trace names the exact line, not the start of the method.

prompt: To run one integration test class, failsafe reads a property: `mvn verify -D___=BooksApiIT`.
Two test classes, each with its own `RANDOM_PORT` context and its own `@BeforeEach` setting `RestAssured.port`, are made to run in parallel in one JVM. What can go wrong?
hint: Look at what kind of field `RestAssured.port` is.

choices.text: The two contexts receive the same port and the second fails to start
choices.why: Each Tomcat asks the operating system for a free port, and two never get the same one.

choices.text: A request of one class reaches the other class's running server
choices.why: Right. The field is static, so it holds the port whichever class set it last, and a test then judges the wrong application.

choices.text: `@LocalServerPort` injects 0 while the other context is starting
choices.why: The port is injected after this context's own server has started, whatever the other one is doing.

choices.text: Nothing, because `@BeforeEach` runs again before every test
choices.why: It does, and the other class's `@BeforeEach` can run between that and the request.

prompt: With no credentials, a client posts a book whose ISBN has a wrong check digit to `/books`. What status comes back?
hint: Which runs first: the filters or the controller's validation?

choices.text: 400, because the ISBN fails `@ValidIsbn`
choices.why: Validation runs when the controller is called, and the request never gets that far.
Right. The security filter chain refuses an unauthenticated request before the controller, so the ISBN is never looked at.

choices.text: 403, because posting books needs the `catalogue:write` scope
choices.why: 403 is for a caller who is known and lacks the scope. This one sent no credentials at all.

choices.text: 201, because the request body is well-formed JSON
choices.why: Well-formed is not enough twice over: no token, and an invalid ISBN.

prompt: `addingABookNeedsAToken` is changed to fetch ana's token first and send it with the book. Which status does the test now get?
hint: Look at ana's authorities in lesson 15's `SecurityConfig`.

choices.text: 201, because the token is valid
choices.why: A valid token says who ana is. Whether she may add books is a separate question.

choices.text: 401, because ana is not the clerk
choices.why: She is authenticated: the token is good. 401 means nobody is known.
Right. Her token carries the scope `orders` only, and `POST /books` needs `catalogue:write`: known, and not allowed.

choices.text: 409, because the ISBN is already in the catalogue
choices.why: 9786500000078 is not one of the six migrated books, and the request never reaches the service anyway.

prompt: In the full `mvn verify`, three PostgreSQL containers started for three integration test classes. If `BookshopApplicationIT` were changed to carry exactly the same three annotations as `BooksApiIT`, how many would start?
hint: Which containers belong to a context, and which contexts can Spring reuse?

prompt: A new test in `BooksApiIT` asserts that book 2 has a stock of 5. It passes when run alone and fails in the full class. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The order test has already taken one copy of book 2 from the same database
choices.why: Right. The class shares one context and one container, and the order is real; the new test depends on which ran first.

choices.text: Flyway runs the migrations again before each test method
choices.why: Flyway runs once, when the context starts. Nothing puts the stock back.

choices.text: Each test method gets its own PostgreSQL container
choices.why: The container is a bean of the context, and the class has one context.

choices.text: REST Assured caches the first answer for `/books/2`
choices.why: REST Assured sends every request; it keeps no cache of answers.

prompt: `sha512sum -c apache-jmeter-5.6.3.tgz.sha512` printed `OK`. What does that establish?

choices.text: That the Apache release manager signed the archive
choices.why: A signature is checked against the `.asc` file and a public key, which this step does not touch.

choices.text: That the bytes match the published hash
choices.why: Right. The download is complete and undamaged. Who made it is the signature's question.

choices.text: That 5.6.3 is the newest release of JMeter
choices.why: A checksum is about one file and says nothing about other releases.

choices.text: That the archive runs on Java 25
choices.why: Which Java it runs on is the program's business; the hash covers bytes only.

prompt: Right after appending the `export PATH=...` line to `~/.bashrc`, `command -v jmeter` in the same terminal prints nothing. Why?

choices.text: The archive was unpacked into the wrong directory
choices.why: `ls ~/opt/apache-jmeter-5.6.3` showed it in place. The shell is the one that has not changed.

choices.text: `command -v` only finds programs that apt installed
choices.why: It searches every directory on `PATH`, whoever put the program there.

choices.text: This shell read `~/.bashrc` before the line existed
choices.why: Right. A shell reads `~/.bashrc` when it starts, so this one still has the old `PATH`. Open a new terminal, or `source ~/.bashrc`, and the line takes effect.

choices.text: The `jmeter` script is not executable until JMeter runs once
choices.why: The archive keeps the script's permissions; it was executable from the moment it was unpacked.

prompt: Match each flag of the `jmeter` command to its job.

pairs.right: the results file, one line per request
build the HTML report when the run ends
delete earlier results and report first
set a property the plan reads with __P

right_distractors: stop the run at the first error

prompt: `books.jmx` is run with `-Jthreads=8 -Jloops=250`. How many requests does the run send?
hint: Count what each thread does on one round.

prompt: Why is the bookshop started with `java -jar` for the load test, rather than run inside `mvn`?

choices.text: Under `mvn` the application ignores `BOOKSHOP_JWT_SECRET`
choices.why: The secret is read from the environment either way.

choices.text: It measures the jar as it ships, without Maven's JVM
choices.why: Right. A load test is a measurement, and whatever else runs on the machine is in it.

choices.text: JMeter can only reach a server started from a jar
choices.why: JMeter sends HTTP to a host and a port; it cannot tell how the server was started.

choices.text: `mvn` would run the load test during `verify`
choices.why: Nothing binds JMeter to a Maven phase here; the plan sits in a directory Maven ignores.

prompt: Somebody empties the `book` table while the plan runs. `/books/search?q=the` now answers `200` with `[]`. What does JMeter record for those samples?
hint: A status is one check. What else does the plan check?

choices.text: Successes, because the status is 200
choices.why: A 200 alone would pass, but the plan also asserts on the body.

choices.text: Successes, though fewer bytes came back
choices.why: The size is recorded, and the samples are still marked failed by the assertion.

choices.text: Nothing: JMeter skips samples whose body is empty
choices.why: Every request becomes a line in the results file, empty body or not.

choices.text: Errors, because the body does not contain `"isbn"`
choices.why: Right. That is the assertion's job: a 200 with the wrong content counts as a failure.

prompt: A report says the 95th percentile of response time was 40 ms. What does that mean?

choices.text: The average request took 40 ms
choices.why: The average is `meanResTime`, a different number; a few slow requests pull it up.

choices.text: 95% of the requests took 40 ms or less
choices.why: Right. The other 5% took longer, and the 99th percentile and the maximum say how much longer.

choices.text: 95% of the requests succeeded within the run
choices.why: Success is the error count. A percentile is about time.

choices.text: The slowest 95 requests averaged 40 ms each
choices.why: A percentile is a position in the sorted times, not an average of a group.

prompt: A plan has 50 threads and no pause between requests. The average response time is 10 ms. Roughly how many requests a second can the run reach?
hint: Each thread sends its next request only when the last one has answered.

prompt: A run reports an average response time of 1 ms and a maximum of 17 ms, better than any run before it. What should you read first?

choices.text: The maximum, to see whether one request was slow
choices.why: The maximum is already the best of any run; slowness is not what went wrong.

choices.text: The 99th percentile, which the average hides
choices.why: Worth reading in a sound run. This one may not have measured the application at all.

choices.text: The error count
choices.why: Right. A refused connection fails at once, so a run against a stopped server has the best response times of all, and every one of them is an error.

choices.text: The ramp-up, which was probably too short
choices.why: Ramp-up changes when threads start, not whether the answers are real.

prompt: JMeter, the bookshop and PostgreSQL all ran on one four-processor machine. Which conclusions can such a run support? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: This commit is slower than the last one, measured with the same plan on the same machine
choices.why: Right. Comparing two versions under identical conditions is what a local run is good for.

choices.text: The response times grow as threads are added on this machine
choices.why: Right. That is a measurement of this machine under this plan, and it says so.

choices.text: The production server will handle the same number of requests a second
choices.why: Production has other processors, other data, a network, and no load generator sharing them.

choices.text: The application, not JMeter, was the limit on throughput
choices.why: JMeter itself used a large share of the same processors, so nothing in this run separates the two.

prompt: Put the steps of a load test you could defend in order.
hint: A number means nothing until you know what it was supposed to be.
items: write down the target, such as a 95th percentile under 50 ms
start the application as it ships
run once to warm it up, and discard that run
read the error count before any time

prompt: Match each failure to the test that would catch it first.

pairs.left: the error handler starts answering application/json
a derived query returns titles in the wrong order
placing an order saves it even when the stock is short
a change makes each search take three times as long

prompt: A REST Assured test for `GET /books/1` checks only `statusCode(200)`. Which regression would it still pass?

choices.text: The route `/books/{id}` is removed
choices.why: Then the answer is a 404 and the status check fails.

choices.text: Reading a book starts to require a token
choices.why: Then the answer is a 401 and the status check fails.

choices.text: The JSON field `title` is renamed to `name`
choices.why: Right. The status stays 200, and every client reading `title` breaks. Only a `body(...)` expectation sees it.

choices.text: The database is unreachable when the test runs
choices.why: Then the context fails to start, or the answer is a 500; either way the test fails.
